title: Drives, Values, and Goals as Domain Translations of Behavioral Control
content: Behavioral control requires translation between different representations. Drives translate physiological state into motivational intensity. Values translate competing drives and context into an ordered ranking. Goals translate current values into temporally extended plans. Each translation defines a protocol for communication between domains. I argue that this need for domain translation shapes behavioral control architecture and its evolutionary patterns of conservation and diversification. Architecturally, drives, values, and goals form a protocol stack, a sequence of translation interfaces of the kind found in robust layered systems in engineering and biology. At each interface, heterogeneous upstream inputs compress into compact signals that downstream systems use to guide action. Failure of translation interrupts communication, concentrating fragility at the interface. Evolutionarily, interfaces tend to be conserved because signal production and interpretation must remain compatible. Conserved interfaces allow upstream inputs and downstream responses to diversify, producing a broad-narrow-broad evolutionary hourglass along each control pathway, analogous to the observed evolutionary hourglass in development. Increasing dependence on internal models from drives to values to goals predicts a gradient from concentrated to distributed translation interfaces and neural circuitry. Drives translate physiology into motivation through concentrated, identifiable interface circuits. Values combine concentrated components for direct translations and distributed components for model-based predictions. Goals rely primarily on distributed circuits for model-based planning. Comparative and experimental observations across vertebrates match the framework's combination of translation, compression, conservation, and fragility.
